guide.title: How to use PeptMass
guide.lead: Interactive demonstrations of the concepts and the workflow. Move the controls: everything is computed live by the same engine as the other screens, without changing your working peptide.
guide.flow.title: The workflow
guide.flow.intro: PeptMass follows one path: define the peptide, predict how it fragments and compare with the measured spectrum. The peptide defined on the Mass screen is kept and the other screens use it.
guide.flow.mass: Type the sequence, apply modifications and see mass, charge states and isotopic envelope.
guide.flow.fragments: Generate the ions the peptide produces in MS/MS and compare with an m/z list.
guide.flow.experimental: Open the instrument file, pick the scan and annotate the spectrum.
guide.flow.library: Register non-natural amino acids and modifications to use in sequences.
guide.mass.title: From sequence to mass
guide.mass.intro: Each letter is an amino acid. PeptMass adds the residue masses plus one water molecule (H2O), which accounts for the free chain ends: H at the N-terminus and OH at the C-terminus.
guide.mass.mono_help: uses only the lightest isotope of each element (12C, 1H, 14N, 16O, 32S). It is the mass of the first peak of the isotopic envelope and the one compared at high resolution.
guide.mass.avg_help: weighted by the natural isotope abundances. It sits near the centre of the envelope and is useful when the instrument does not resolve isotopes.
guide.charge.title: Charge and m/z
guide.charge.intro: In electrospray ionization (ESI), the peptide usually gains z protons and becomes [M+zH]z+. The spectrometer does not measure mass, it measures the mass-to-charge ratio (m/z): the higher the charge, the lower the observed m/z.
guide.charge.table: The same molecule at different charges (m/z)
guide.iso.title: Isotopic envelope
guide.iso.intro: About 1.1% of natural carbon is 13C. That is why each peptide appears as a group of peaks, the isotopic envelope, spaced by about 1 Da (divided by the charge, in m/z). The first peak, M, is the monoisotopic one. Increase the size and watch the envelope change.
guide.iso.top_mono: The most intense peak is the monoisotopic one (M).
guide.iso.top_other: The most intense peak is already M+{k}. In large peptides the monoisotopic peak becomes small, and mixing up the peaks causes an error of about 1 Da in the mass.
guide.iso.limit: The demonstration goes up to about 15 kDa. Above about 20 kDa, the envelope computed by PeptMass still cuts off the most intense peak (known limitation).
guide.frag.title: Fragmentation
guide.frag.intro: In MS/MS the precursor is fragmented, mainly at the peptide bonds. The piece holding the N-terminus gives a, b or c ions; the piece holding the C-terminus gives x, y or z. The number tells how many residues the fragment has. CID and HCD mostly give b and y; ETD gives c and z.
guide.frag.click: Hover, click or Tab through the bonds between residues.
guide.frag.need: Compute a valid peptide in section 1.
guide.frag.spectrum: Theoretical spectrum of both series (chosen cleavage highlighted)
guide.tol.title: Matching and tolerance
guide.tol.intro: An experimental peak matches a theoretical ion when their difference is within the tolerance. On high-resolution instruments it is given in ppm (parts per million), which scales with m/z.
guide.tol.formula: error (ppm) = (experimental m/z - theoretical m/z) / theoretical m/z × 1,000,000
guide.tol.simulated: Spectrum simulated from the b and y ions (charge 1+) of the peptide above: every real peak has a small measurement error, there are noise peaks, and one ion is missing, with a noise peak close to it. Move the tolerance and see what matches.
guide.tol.tight: Tolerance too tight: {n} ion(s) present in the spectrum were left out.
guide.tol.loose: Tolerance too loose: ion {ion} matched a noise peak, but it does not exist in this spectrum. It is a false positive.
guide.tol.good: Every ion present matched and no noise got in.
guide.exp.title: Experimental data, step by step
guide.exp.intro: The bundled example file is synthetic, with the b and y ions of PEPTIDE. With it you can run the whole workflow without your own data.
guide.exp.step1: On the Experimental data screen, open the file (.mzML, .mzXML or Thermo .raw). The TIC chromatogram appears.
guide.exp.step2: Click the chromatogram to pick a scan. To find the peptide, build the XIC at the precursor m/z.
guide.exp.step3: Choose series and charges and click Match with fragments. The peptide used is the one from the Mass screen.
guide.exp.step4: Read the result: annotated peaks in each series colour, score, criteria and the ion table.
guide.exp.try_help: Sets the working peptide to PEPTIDE and opens the Experimental data screen with the example file loaded.
guide.exp.criteria: How to read the identification criteria
guide.exp.c_precursor: The scan precursor m/z, converted to mass using the charge, must agree with the peptide mass. The limit is the tolerance itself when it is in ppm, or 20 ppm when it is in Da.
guide.exp.c_isotopes: The precursor envelope in the preceding MS1 must resemble the theoretical one: cosine of at least 0.90, with 2 or more aligned isotopes. Below that the criterion only warns (~).
guide.exp.c_rt: Only checked if you enter the expected RT; the scan must fall inside the window.
guide.exp.c_note: These limits are PeptMass choices, inspired by the identification criteria used in anti-doping. They are not the official WADA rules.
guide.exp.score: it is the Morpheus score: the number of matched ions plus the fraction of the scan total ion current (TIC) they explain. It compares candidates on the same scan; it is not a probability.
guide.exp.chart: grey peaks were not annotated. Annotated peaks have their series colour, and only the 15 most intense are labelled; drag to zoom and see the rest. Hover a peak for details.
guide.gloss.title: Glossary
guide.g.da.d: Unit of molecular mass: 1/12 of the mass of a 12C atom. 1 kDa = 1,000 Da.
guide.g.mz.d: Ratio between the mass and the charge of the ion. It is what the spectrometer measures on the horizontal axis.
guide.g.mono.d: Mass computed with only the lightest isotope of each element. It is the first peak of the envelope.
guide.g.avg.d: Mass weighted by the natural isotope abundances. Useful at low resolution.
guide.g.charge.d: Number of charges on the ion; in positive ESI, usually the number of protons gained.
guide.g.ppm.d: Parts per million: relative mass error. 10 ppm at m/z 1,000 is 0.01.
guide.g.envelope.d: Group of peaks of the same molecule with different numbers of heavy isotopes, mainly 13C.
guide.g.ms1ms2.d: MS1 measures intact ions; MS2 isolates a precursor, fragments it and measures the fragments.
guide.g.precursor.d: Ion isolated in MS1 to be fragmented in MS2.
guide.g.ions.t: a, b, c, x, y, z ions
guide.g.ions.d: Peptide fragments: a, b and c hold the N-terminus; x, y and z, the C-terminus. CID and HCD mostly give b and y; ETD, c and z.
guide.g.loss.d: Fragment that lost an uncharged molecule, such as H2O (18.011 Da) or NH3 (17.027 Da).
guide.g.nc.d: The two chain ends: the free amino group (N) and the free carboxyl group (C).
guide.g.mod.d: Chemical change on a residue or chain end, such as acetylation, amidation, oxidation or phosphorylation, that changes the mass.
guide.g.nonnatural.d: Residue outside the standard 20, such as Aib. In PeptMass it is registered in the Library by its formula.
guide.g.tic.d: Total ion current: the sum of the intensities of each scan over time.
guide.g.xic.d: Extracted ion chromatogram: intensity of a specific m/z, within a tolerance, over time.
guide.g.rt.d: Time at which the compound leaves the liquid chromatography and reaches the spectrometer.
guide.g.centroid.d: Profile keeps the continuous signal of each peak; centroid reduces each peak to one point (m/z and intensity).
guide.g.morpheus.d: Number of matched ions plus the fraction of the scan TIC they explain (Wenger and Coon, 2013).
